(i) Classification of methods of statistical analysis

column2: Collecting, organising, summarising and presenting data: tables, graphs, measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode), dispersion (range, variance, standard deviation) and shape.
When the aim is only to describe the data at hand, e.g. summarising a class's exam scores, census results or monthly sales.
Using a sample to draw conclusions about a population, with a measure of uncertainty: estimation (point and interval), hypothesis testing, regression and correlation.
When studying the whole population is impossible, too costly, too slow or destructive, e.g. opinion polls, clinical trials, quality control, forecasting.
z-test, t-test, ANOVA: used for interval/ratio data when the population distribution (usually normal) can be assumed.
Chi-square, sign test, Mann–Whitney, Spearman's rank: used for nominal/ordinal data, small samples, or when distributional assumptions fail.
Univariate (one variable), bivariate (relationship between two, e.g. correlation) and multivariate (three or more, e.g. multiple regression).

column1: (ii) Need for Statistics in BA Economics, and the role of a statistician

column2: Economics is built on data (GDP, inflation, unemployment, prices, household surveys). Statistics is needed to collect, summarise and present such data correctly.
It is the foundation of econometrics: estimating relationships such as demand, consumption and production functions, and testing economic theories against real data.
It supports forecasting (growth, inflation, exchange rates) and evaluating the impact of policies such as taxes, subsidies and interest-rate changes.
It helps in decision-making under uncertainty, and in critically reading economic reports, research papers and official statistics.
Data analysis skills are in high demand in banks, government, research institutes and business, so they improve employability.
Planning and design: states objectives as testable hypotheses, chooses the sampling/experimental design and sample size, uses randomisation to reduce bias.
Data collection: designs questionnaires and instruments; ensures the data are accurate and representative.
Data processing: cleans and organises the data; deals with errors, missing values and outliers.
Analysis: chooses and applies appropriate statistical methods and checks their assumptions.
Interpretation and reporting: draws valid conclusions, states confidence/significance and limitations, and presents results clearly for decision-makers.
